components.name: Password hashing & session management (data/store.js)
components.purpose: Authenticate users and maintain login sessions without leaking credentials or blocking the server.
components.design:
Current scrypt params (N=16384, r=8, p=1, keylen=64, ~16MB working set) meet the OWASP floor and are acceptable; timingSafeEqual is used correctly for the hash comparison. Two real defects to fix:

1) EVENT-LOOP BLOCKING (the most serious item). `crypto.scryptSync` runs synchronously on Node's single JS thread, not the libuv threadpool. Each login/signup blocks ALL other request handling (nearby search, static files, every other user's login) for the full derivation time (~40-100ms). Under concurrent logins — or an attacker simply firing many login requests — these calls serialize and the whole app stalls; this is a real, easy denial-of-service, not a theoretical one, because Node is single-threaded for JS execution. FIX: switch to the async/Promise form (`util.promisify(crypto.scrypt)` or the native Promise-returning variant), make `hashPassword`/`verifyPassword`/`createUser`/login async, and `await` them in server.js. Async scrypt runs on the libuv threadpool (default 4 threads), keeping the main thread free to route unrelated requests. Pair this with a small in-process concurrency cap (e.g. semaphore limiting in-flight scrypt verifications to ~4-8) so a burst of logins can't starve the threadpool that `fsp.writeFile` (store saves) also depends on; also consider raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.

2) LOGIN TIMING/ENUMERATION: `ok = user && store.verifyPassword(...)` short-circuits when the email doesn't exist, skipping the expensive scrypt call — this creates a timing side-channel that distinguishes existing vs non-existing emails even though the JSON error message is identical. Combined with the /api/auth/signup 409 ("An account with that email already exists") this makes email enumeration trivial anyway, so the fix is secondary but should still be done for defense-in-depth: run a dummy scrypt derivation (fixed cost) on the not-found path so response timing is constant.

3) THROTTLING GAP: `attemptKey = ip:email` means an attacker rotating the email on each request (or rotating source IP against one target email) escapes the 8-attempts/15-min limiter entirely — there is no per-email-only ceiling independent of IP. Add a second counter keyed by email alone (lower ceiling, longer window, e.g. 20/hour) so credential stuffing against one account can't be IP-laundered. Also note `req.socket.remoteAddress` is meaningless if ever deployed behind a reverse proxy without properly-trusted X-Forwarded-For handling — flag this as a hard prerequisite for whoever owns deployment.

4) SESSION MECHANICS are otherwise sound: opaque random 32-byte token in an HttpOnly cookie, only the sha256 digest persisted (a stolen store.json doesn't hand out live session tokens), fresh token minted on every login (no fixation), and TTL-based expiry with `pruneSessions()`. Missing pieces: no way to invalidate all sessions for a user (needed once a password-change/account-deletion flow exists — add a userId index or linear-scan `destroyAllSessionsForUser`) and no "log out of other devices" endpoint.

components.name: Friend request model (data/store.js, /api/friends/*)
components.purpose: Mutual-accept friending with zero stranger discovery.
components.design:
The core state machine (pending → accepted/declined, `areFriends` via sorted-key friendship lookup) is structurally fine, but has real abuse holes:

1) NO COOLDOWN AFTER DECLINE: once a request is declined, `pendingRequestBetween` no longer matches it (only 'pending' status counts) and `areFriends` is false, so the decliner can be re-requested immediately, repeatedly, forever. This is a harassment vector (repeated notifications/pressure). Fix: after a decline, block re-requests from that sender for a cooldown window (e.g. 30 days) unless the RECIPIENT re-initiates, tracked via a `cooldownUntil` on the request or a small `declines` table keyed by pair.

2) ACCOUNT ENUMERATION ORACLE (explicitly flagged as needing a fix): `POST /api/friends/request` returns 404 "No account with that email" on a miss and 201 on success — this lets anyone iterate candidate emails and learn who has an account, directly contradicting the app's own "no stranger discovery" design goal. FIX: collapse every outcome (no such account, already friends, already pending, blocked) into one identical response, e.g. `200 {ok:true, message:"If that email has an account, they'll see your request."}`, and make the request creation itself idempotent/silent-no-op internally for all of those cases so behavior is indistinguishable from outside. Also add a per-sender rate limit on this endpoint (e.g. 20/day) since even a generic response can be enumerated via response *timing* if the DB lookup path differs in cost — pad/normalize.

3) BLOCKING INTERACTION (see blocking component): once blocking exists, `sendFriendRequest` must consult `isBlocked` and fold that into the same generic response — a blocked sender must see nothing different from a nonexistent-account response, otherwise the block itself becomes an oracle.

4) MISSING: no way to cancel your own outgoing pending request (`POST /api/friends/cancel`), and no request expiry/pagination — low severity but should be added.

Race conditions are not a real concern here since Node is single-threaded and there's no `await` between the check and the `db.friendRequests.push`/save enqueue, so check-then-act is effectively atomic within one request.

components.name: Location privacy & sharing (the critical section)
components.purpose: Let a user share an approximate current location with specific mutually-friended people, never publicly, with real revocability.
components.design:
The current design (per-friend opt-in share, default OFF, requires `areFriends`, coordinates rounded to 2 decimal places ≈1.1km, only the single latest position retained — no history log) has the right instincts but is NOT sufficient on its own as a persistent, always-on feature. Concrete gaps and required fixes:

1) STATIC ROUNDING IS A WEAK FUZZ METHOD. `fuzz()` deterministically snaps to the nearest 0.01° grid cell. Repeated samples while the user is stationary (e.g. asleep at home) ALL land on the exact same value — a single observation already pins the 1.1km×1.1km cell, and it never gets noisier with more samples, but the real threat isn't the cell size, it's that a friend who can query this endpoint repeatedly over hours/days can reconstruct a full behavioral routine (home cell every night, work cell every weekday) — a bounded fuzz radius protects an exact address but does nothing against pattern-of-life tracking, which is the realistic stalking threat model for a location-sharing feature. TREAT THE FIX AS TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, not one: (a) spatial fuzz radius, (b) temporal exposure window.

2) REQUIRED: AUTO-EXPIRY OF SHARED LOCATION. This is the single highest-leverage fix. A `share` toggle must not mean "track me forever once flipped on." Change `shares[key]` from a bare boolean to `{ enabled, updatedAt, expiresAt }`, default expiry short (e.g. 2-8 hours, user-selectable at share time — "share for 1h / until I turn it off"), and have `friendLocations()` filter out any share past its `expiresAt` AND filter out any location reading older than a staleness threshold (e.g. 30-60 min) even if the share itself hasn't expired — a stale pin is misleading and should disappear rather than showing a frozen last-known dot. "Share forever" should still exist as an explicit option but should require periodic re-confirmation (e.g. a banner every N days: "You're still sharing your location with X — keep sharing?").

3) CONSENT UX / VISIBILITY: build a dedicated "Who can see my location" view driven by `db.shares` filtered to `ownerId = me`, each row one-tap revocable, AND a separate "whose location can I see" view — both directions need explicit surfaces; a boolean flipped once in a settings menu with no ongoing visibility is not real informed consent for a feature this sensitive.

4) REVOCATION: `setShare(false)` deleting the key is correct and immediate server-side — `friendLocations` stops returning it on the very next call. The residual gap is purely client-side polling latency (a friend's already-open map won't clear the pin until their next poll); document a bounded poll interval (e.g. 60s) while a friends-map view is open, and add `DELETE /api/location` so a user can immediately wipe their last-known position (useful right before or instead of relying on expiry).

5) UNTHROTTLED WRITE PATH: `POST /api/location` currently has no rate limiting at all (unlike /api/friends and the Places routes) and every `save()` call does a full synchronous `JSON.stringify` of the entire store and a file write. A chatty or malicious client can hammer this endpoint. Add both a per-IP/per-user throttle (e.g. 1 accepted update per 20-30s) and reject faster updates with a cheap 429 before even touching the store.

6) Net recommendation: keep the 2dp spatial fuzz (reasonable, roughly matches what consumer location-sharing apps use) but do NOT treat it as sufficient alone — the auto-expiry + staleness filtering + explicit "who can see me" UI are load-bearing, not optional polish, given the owner's own stated goal (no stranger tracking, friends-only) would otherwise be undermined by a friends-only feature that behaves like persistent surveillance once toggled on.

components.name: Blocking & reporting (currently absent — must be added)
components.purpose: Give a user a way to stop unwanted contact and flag abusive accounts, independent of the friend graph.
components.design:
New store.js collections:
```
blocks:  [{ id, blockerId, blockedId, createdAt }]
reports: [{ id, reporterId, reportedUserId, reason, details, createdAt, status: 'open'|'reviewed'|'actioned' }]
```
Behavior:
- `isBlocked(a,b)` checks either direction and must gate `sendFriendRequest` (folded into the same generic non-committal response used for account enumeration — a block must never be distinguishable from "no such account").
- Blocking immediately: removes any existing friendship between the pair, deletes both directions of `db.shares`, and cancels/removes any pending friend request between them — done synchronously as one operation, no partial state.
- Blocking is silent — the blocked user gets no notification.
- Reporting does not require friendship (harassment can happen via repeated blocked requests alone) and should default to also auto-blocking the reported user for the reporter (standard UX pattern, should be overridable).
- Rate-limit `POST /api/reports` (e.g. 5/day/user) so the report channel itself can't be used to spam.
- Given the app has zero admin UI or dependencies, the owner needs *some* way to see open reports — cheapest option consistent with the zero-dep constraint: a `GET /api/admin/reports` endpoint gated to the seed/owner account id (not a role system, just `user.id === SEED_ID` check), or a small read-only script that dumps the `reports` array from store.json. Flag this as a gap that needs an explicit decision — reports collected with no review path are useless.
Endpoints: `GET /api/blocks`, `POST /api/blocks {userId}`, `DELETE /api/blocks/:userId`, `POST /api/reports {userId, reason, details}`.

components.name: Cookie/session hardening & CSRF posture
components.purpose: Ensure the session cookie and mutating endpoints can't be driven cross-site.
components.design:
SameSite=Lax + HttpOnly already blocks the cookie from being attached to cross-site POST/fetch requests, which covers classic CSRF for every mutating endpoint regardless of the JSON content-type check — that check is real but secondary defense-in-depth (it stops SameSite-bypass edge cases: old browsers, misconfigured proxies stripping the SameSite header, or the app later being embedded/iframed). The actionable gap: **the JSON-content-type gate currently only exists in `handleAuth`** (signup/login) — `handleFriends`, `handleLocation`, and `handleSaved` accept POST/DELETE bodies without checking `content-type`, so if SameSite protection is ever weakened for any reason, the higher-value endpoints (friend requests, location-share toggling, saved places) have no secondary defense at all. Fix: factor the content-type check into one shared helper and apply it uniformly to every mutating route, not just auth.

Secondary items:
- `COOKIE_SECURE` defaults to OFF unless an env var explicitly sets it to '1' — this is an unsafe default. If a production deploy forgets that one env var, session cookies go out over plain HTTP. Flip the default: require an explicit opt-OUT for local dev (e.g. `COOKIE_SECURE=0`) rather than opt-in for prod, or auto-detect via `x-forwarded-proto`.
- No CORS headers are set anywhere, so cross-origin `fetch()` reads of any `/api/*` GET response are blocked by the browser regardless of the cookie — GET-based data leakage is not currently exploitable; keep it that way (don't add permissive CORS later without revisiting this).
- Add `destroyAllSessionsForUser` + a "log out everywhere" endpoint for future password-change/account-deletion flows (currently sessions have no userId index for bulk revoke).
- `/api/location` and `/api/saved` are the only mutating routes with NO per-IP rate limiting at all in the dispatch table (`/api/friends` and the Places routes have it) — add it to close that gap, both for abuse resistance and to bound `store.save()` write frequency.

components.name: Legal surface: Privacy Policy & Terms of Use
components.purpose: Disclose exactly what's collected/shared for a GPS + social-graph app, and give users real control over their data.
components.design:
Must specifically cover, in plain language:
- What's collected: name, email, hashed password (never plaintext/exportable), friend graph, saved places, and — only if location sharing is used — a fuzzed (~1.1km) *single most-recent* location with NO history retained server-side (this is a real privacy positive worth stating explicitly).
- Exactly how fuzzing + the new auto-expiry work, and that turning sharing off (or letting it expire) removes the data from friends' view immediately.
- That Google Places/Maps/Geocoding APIs receive server-side queries (coordinates or free-text address) proxied through buisnessfind's own server key — no user name/email is ever sent to Google — with a link to Google's own privacy policy for how they treat that traffic.
- IP addresses are used only in-memory for rate-limiting and are never persisted to disk (true today — keep it true).
- User rights: access, export, and delete. Concretely implement `GET /api/account/export` (dumps the user's own user/friendships/requests/savedPlaces/location, minus password hash) and `DELETE /api/account` (cascading delete across users, sessions, friendRequests both directions, friendships both directions + counterpart shares, locations, savedPlaces, blocks; reports where they were the reporter can be anonymized rather than fully deleted for trust & safety continuity).
- Minimum age self-attestation checkbox at signup (e.g. 13+/16+ depending on target jurisdiction), persisted as `ageConfirmed`/`termsAcceptedAt` on the user record for audit purposes — signup currently has no such consent capture at all.
- Terms of Use should explicitly prohibit using location/friend features to stalk or harass, describe the block/report mechanism, disclaim that fuzzed location is approximate and unsuitable for safety-critical/emergency use, and disclaim liability for third-party (Google) review content accuracy.

components.name: Final data model & endpoint list
components.purpose: Single source of truth for what store.js and server.js need to expose once all the above is applied.
components.design:
store.json shape (additions marked NEW):
```
users: [{ id, name, email, password, createdAt, ageConfirmed(NEW), termsAcceptedAt(NEW) }]
sessions: { digest -> { userId, expires, createdAt(NEW) } }
friendRequests: [{ id, fromId, toId, status: pending|accepted|declined|cancelled(NEW), createdAt, respondedAt(NEW), cooldownUntil(NEW) }]
friendships: [{ id, userA, userB, createdAt }]
shares: { 'owner:friend' -> { enabled, updatedAt, expiresAt(NEW) } }  // was a bare boolean
locations: { userId -> { lat, lng, updatedAt } }  // unchanged shape, now staleness-filtered on read
savedPlaces: [...]
apiUsage: {...}
blocks: [{ id, blockerId, blockedId, createdAt }]      // NEW
reports: [{ id, reporterId, reportedUserId, reason, details, createdAt, status }]  // NEW
```
Endpoints (NEW ones marked):
Auth: POST /api/auth/signup (now requires ageConfirmed+agreedToTerms), POST /api/auth/login, POST /api/auth/logout, POST /api/auth/logout-all (NEW), GET /api/auth/me.
Friends: GET /api/friends, POST /api/friends/request (generic-response, blocked-aware), POST /api/friends/cancel (NEW), POST /api/friends/accept, POST /api/friends/decline, POST /api/friends/remove, GET /api/friends/locations (expiry+staleness filtered), POST /api/friends/share {friendId, share, expiresInHours} (expiry-aware).
Location: POST /api/location (rate-limited), DELETE /api/location (NEW).
Blocks/Reports (NEW): GET /api/blocks, POST /api/blocks, DELETE /api/blocks/:userId, POST /api/reports.
Saved: GET/POST/DELETE /api/saved (now rate-limited).
Account (NEW): GET /api/account/export, DELETE /api/account.
Places (unchanged): /api/config, /api/nearby, /api/place, /api/geocode.
All mutating routes share: requireUser, the JSON-content-type CSRF gate, and per-IP+per-user rate limiting — applied uniformly rather than only on /api/auth and /api/friends as today.

risks: scryptSync blocks Node's single JS thread (not the threadpool) — concurrent or attacker-driven login bursts can stall the entire app (all users, all endpoints), not just other logins; this is the highest-priority fix (switch to async scrypt + a concurrency cap).

POST /api/friends/request returns a different response for a nonexistent email (404) vs success (201) vs presumably a distinct error for already-friends/already-pending — this is a direct account-enumeration oracle that contradicts the app's own 'no stranger discovery' design goal; must collapse to one generic response for every outcome including future block state.
Declined friend requests can be resent immediately and indefinitely by the same sender — no cooldown exists, enabling repeated-request harassment against someone who has already said no.
No blocking mechanism exists at all — a user has no way to stop someone from friend-requesting them short of repeatedly declining, and no reporting/moderation path exists for abusive accounts.

Location fuzzing (2dp rounding) only bounds the error radius per-sample; it does nothing to prevent pattern-of-life tracking from repeated, unthrottled observation over time. Without auto-expiry of shares and staleness filtering of stale readings, a 'friends-only' toggle behaves like persistent surveillance once switched on, which undercuts the owner's stated privacy goal.

POST /api/location and the /api/saved endpoints have no per-IP/per-user rate limiting at all in the dispatch table, unlike /api/friends and the Places routes — both an abuse vector and, for location specifically, a privacy-relevant gap (unbounded update frequency).

The JSON-content-type CSRF defense is only applied to /api/auth/* — friends/location/saved mutating endpoints have no equivalent secondary defense if SameSite protection is ever weakened (proxy misconfiguration, legacy browser, future embedding).
COOKIE_SECURE defaults to off (opt-in), meaning a production deploy that forgets to set the env var will transmit session cookies over plain HTTP.

Login attempt throttling is keyed by ip:email, so an attacker can bypass it entirely by rotating the email per request, or by rotating source IPs against one target email — there is no per-email-only ceiling.

req.socket.remoteAddress is used directly for all IP-based rate limiting; if ever deployed behind a reverse proxy without correctly trusted X-Forwarded-For handling, every per-IP throttle in the app (login, friends, location, places) becomes either globally over-applied (all users share the proxy's IP) or spoofable.

No account export/delete endpoints exist yet, and no consent capture (age, terms acceptance) happens at signup — both are likely required before public launch given the sensitivity of location + social-graph data.

Once a password-change or account-deletion flow is added, there is currently no way to bulk-invalidate a user's other sessions (sessions aren't indexed by userId) — flagging now so it isn't retrofitted awkwardly later.
summary: Reviewed data/store.js and server.js end to end. The scrypt/session core is structurally sound (correct timingSafeEqual usage, opaque tokens with only a sha256 digest persisted, fresh token per login) but has one serious operational risk — scryptSync blocks Node's single JS thread, so concurrent logins can stall the entire app — plus a login-throttle bypass via email rotation. The friends model correctly enforces mutual-accept with no stranger discovery in the happy path, but /api/friends/request leaks account existence via its error response (a direct enumeration oracle contradicting the app's own privacy goal), and declined requests can be resent forever with no cooldown. Location privacy is the most consequential gap: 2-decimal-place rounding bounds per-sample error but does nothing against repeated-observation pattern-of-life tracking once a share is toggled on, and there is currently no auto-expiry, no staleness filtering, no 'who can see me' visibility UI, and no rate limit on location updates — these are load-bearing fixes, not polish, given the owner's explicit friends-only/no-tracking intent. Blocking and reporting are entirely absent and need a new data model. CSRF defense (JSON content-type gate) is applied only to auth routes, not to friends/location/saved, and COOKIE_SECURE defaults unsafely to off. No legal surface (privacy policy, terms, consent capture, export/delete) exists yet despite the app handling GPS location and a social graph. Full data model and endpoint additions are specified in the components below, with every finding treated adversarially against a stalking/tracking threat model as instructed.
